Roald Amundsen was a Norwegian explorer who achieved both the Northwest Passage and the South Pole, becoming the first person to reach the South Pole in December 1911. His systematic, methodical approach to polar exploration—including careful planning, use of dog sleds, and superior supply management—contrasted sharply with European traditions and proved more effective in the harsh polar environment.

He first successfully navigated the Northwest Passage between 1903 and 1906, confirming the existence of the route that polar explorers had sought for centuries. When he heard that Frederick Cook and Robert Peary had already reached the North Pole, he changed his expedition's destination from the Arctic to the South Pole. He led a five-man team to the South Pole in December 1911, beating Robert Falcon Scott's British expedition by about a month.

Unlike Europeans who followed tradition, Amundsen used dog teams extensively, following indigenous Inuit practices rather than man-hauling sleds, which proved far more efficient. He was meticulous in pre-positioning supply depots along his route, allowing his team to travel with minimal loads and preserve energy. After returning safely to civilization, he spent years lecturing, writing, and conducting Arctic expeditions. He sought the North Pole by airship, but disappeared in 1928 while attempting a rescue mission for an Arctic airship, dying near the North Pole he had spent years pursuing. His death came as a tragic end to an explorer's life.
